newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Go outside Europe's core for EMU plays.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Go outside Europe's core for EMU plays.

text.p: European core bonds offer little scope for convergence trades but a few markets at the "edge" of the core look attractive as preparations for European economic and monetary union gather momentum, analysts said on Tuesday.
European Union finance ministers hold an "Ecofin" meeting in Dublin this weekend, bringing EMU-based strategies into focus.

But while countries such as France, Belgium and the Netherlands -- all trading close to 10-year Bunds -- will fail to excite investors, markets such as Finnish and Irish bonds have more potential, they said. Ecu bonds also look intriguing.
"The core of Europe has already converged. I don't think there's enough return enhancement to justify divestment from Germany," said Steve Major, Paris-based head of bond research at Credit Lyonnais.
"The first priority I would have thought would be to diversify into Ecu which has been happening over the last two to three weeks in front of this Ecofin meeting," Major said.
The 10-year spread of Ecu bonds over Bunds has narrowed to 45 basis points currently from around 60 a few weeks ago. Major said it could fall another 15 basis points.

Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London, said that if authorities could agree on a so-called stability pact at the weekend, it would bolster core European debt in general but he too doubted there were good spread trades there.

"It's getting quite tricky because we have to ask what would be the spread under EMU. I would argue it probably won't be more than five or 10 basis points for Belgium if it's in. So the upside for Belgium is probably limited," Schmidt said.
The Belgian/Bund spread was quoted around 22 basis points.
Similarly, French yields would trade close to parity with Germany, but trades such as these -- for five or 10 basis points of yield pickup -- were not worth it, he said.
Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London, concurred. "There's not a lot of incentive to be holding the French market when it's trading flat to Germany."
European officials have said there is a good chance of reaching agreement soon on a stability pact, which would be designed to set out fiscal discipline measures for countries under EMU.
"An EMU with a stability pact, which has effective sanctions on those deficits, would be likely to have lower interest rates than one without those sanctions," Schmidt said.

That is because without sanctions there would be an incentive for some countries to loosen their guard on public finances and that would lead to more general fiscal deterioration in Europe. That in turn would put pressure on interest rates.

Major said he saw a possible group of eight countries as initial members of EMU -- Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, Ireland and Finland. Of those, the last two were more doubtful and their yield spreads as a result gave more room for convergence.
Even more attractive, he argued, was Spain, which was yielding some 216 basis points over Germany and which he believes could narrow the spread to 150 or lower.
Bevan, however, said he would look at the U.S. as a possible alternative to European debt, albeit for reasons that had little to do with EMU proceedings.
"There's been this apparent decoupling between Europe and the U.S. German bond yields are actually lower than six months ago, whereas in the U.S. bond yields are quite a bit higher."
But while fundamental conditions for decoupling made sense six months ago, Bevan was not so sure they existed now.
"I am wondering whether this might represent a better opportunity to make a strategic shift out of Europe into the U.S. Fundamentally, the German market starts to look a bit stretched," he said.
